front.title: Upper vs. lower airway
front.summary: The dividing line is the larynx.

back.body: Upper: nose, mouth, pharynx (naso, oro, laryngo), epiglottis, larynx with vocal cords. Lower: trachea, carina, right and left bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli. Gas exchange only in alveoli. Cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring.
back.why_it_matters: Structure names show up as distractors for each other; know which side of the line each sits on.

front.title: The tongue is the obstruction
front.summary: In the unresponsive supine patient, assume the tongue first.

back.body: Loss of muscle tone → tongue falls back against the posterior pharynx → snoring, partial or complete obstruction. Fix: head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw-thrust, then an airway adjunct to hold it.
back.why_it_matters: The most common obstruction has the simplest fix, and it is the first airway skill you learn.

front.title: Adult vs. pediatric airway
front.summary: Smaller, softer, more crowded, less reserve.

back.body: Child: large tongue, large occiput (pad under shoulders), narrow airway, narrowest at cricoid, high anterior larynx, floppy U-shaped epiglottis, soft trachea (no hyperextension), fast desaturation. Head tilt: slight for children, neutral for infants.
back.why_it_matters: Every difference is tested, and every difference changes how you position the head.

front.title: Pad the shoulders
front.summary: Why an infant's airway folds when they lie flat.

back.body: The large occiput tips the chin toward the chest and flexes the neck. A folded towel under the shoulders levels the head so the ear canal lines up with the front of the shoulder. Neutral position, no tilt.
back.why_it_matters: The classic pediatric airway question, and a real fix you will use on every unresponsive infant.

front.title: Ventilation, respiration, oxygenation
front.summary: Three different things that fail separately.

back.body: Ventilation: moving air (chest rise). Respiration: gas exchange at the alveoli and at the cells. Oxygenation: oxygen onto hemoglobin and out to tissues. CO poisoning = ventilating, not oxygenating. Slow shallow breathing = not ventilating, CO2 builds up.
back.why_it_matters: The exam asks which one is broken, and chest rise alone never answers that.

front.title: Breathing volumes
front.summary: Tidal volume, dead space, minute volume.

back.body: Tidal volume ~500 mL (adult) · Dead space ~150 mL · Minute volume = TV × rate, normal ~6 to 8 L/min · Alveolar ventilation = (TV − 150) × rate · Normal drive to breathe = rising CO2
back.why_it_matters: Explains why shallow breathing is worse than the rate suggests.

front.title: Normal respiratory rates
front.summary: By age. Memorize all three.

back.body: Adult 12 to 20 · Child (1 to 12 yr) 15 to 30 · Infant (under 1 yr) 25 to 50 · Count 30 seconds × 2 without telling the patient · Normal = regular, even chest rise, quiet, effortless, full sentences
back.why_it_matters: A rate of 28 is normal in a toddler and abnormal in an adult; the exam will ask both.

front.title: Adequate vs. inadequate breathing
front.summary: The decision the whole airway module builds toward.

back.body: Adequate: normal rate for age, regular, even chest rise, quiet, easy, full sentences → oxygen if hypoxic. Inadequate: rate too fast or slow, shallow, irregular, accessory muscles, retractions, flaring, tripod, 2 to 3 word dyspnea → ventilate with BVM. Late: cyanosis, altered mental status, agonal gasps (= not breathing).
back.why_it_matters: Oxygen versus ventilation is the single most important airway decision at the EMT level.

front.title: Signs of effort
front.summary: What working hard to breathe looks like.

back.body: Accessory muscle use (neck, shoulders) · Retractions (skin pulling in between or under ribs) · Nasal flaring · Tripod position · Pursed-lip breathing · Two or three words per breath · Cannot lie flat
back.why_it_matters: Effort is where you catch inadequate breathing before the late signs appear.

front.title: Head-tilt/chin-lift
front.summary: The default way to open an airway when the spine is not a concern

back.body: Hand on the forehead, tilt back · Fingertips lift the BONY chin · Never press the soft tissue under the jaw · The tongue is attached to the jaw, so moving the jaw moves the tongue · Not used when the mechanism suggests spinal injury
back.why_it_matters: The tongue is the most common airway obstruction in an unresponsive patient, and this fixes it with no equipment.

front.title: Jaw-thrust
front.summary: Open the airway without moving the neck

back.body: Kneel at the head · Fingers behind both angles of the jaw · Push the jaw forward, head stays neutral · Tiring, and usually needs a second rescuer to bag · If it will not open the airway, an open airway still wins
back.why_it_matters: The maneuver is chosen by the mechanism of injury, not by how the patient looks.

front.title: Head-tilt/chin-lift vs. jaw-thrust
front.summary: Same goal, two routes

back.body: Both bring the jaw forward so the tongue clears the back of the throat. The chin-lift tilts the head to do it; the jaw-thrust pushes from behind the angles of the jaw and leaves the head where it is. The mechanism of injury decides which you use.
back.why_it_matters: This pairing is a mechanism question dressed up as an airway question.

front.title: Recovery position
front.summary: For the unresponsive patient who is breathing fine

back.body: Unresponsive + breathing adequately + no suspected spinal injury · Roll as a unit, head supported, mouth lowest · Lets vomit and secretions drain out instead of down · Not for trauma mechanisms · Not a substitute for reassessment
back.why_it_matters: Position buys drainage, not safety — you still stay at the head with suction ready.

front.title: Oropharyngeal airway
front.summary: Holds the tongue so your hands are free

back.body: Corner of the mouth to the earlobe or angle of the jaw · NO gag reflex, ever · Adult: tip toward the roof of the mouth, rotate 180 degrees · Child: tongue depressor, insert right side up, do not rotate · Too long presses the epiglottis; too short leaves the tongue in the way
back.why_it_matters: The gag reflex question and the sizing landmarks are both guaranteed exam material.

front.title: Inserting an OPA
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: confirm no gag reflex, measure against the patient, confirm the flange sits at the lips, keep the head positioned afterwards.
back.why_it_matters: Sizing by eye and missing a gag reflex are the two things that fail this station.

front.title: Nasopharyngeal airway
front.summary: The adjunct a gagging patient will accept

back.body: Tip of the nose to the earlobe · Water-soluble lubricant only · Bevel toward the septum · Advance STRAIGHT BACK along the nasal floor, not up · Avoid with significant head or mid-face trauma · Does not protect against vomit
back.why_it_matters: Aiming the tube upward is the single most common insertion error.

front.title: Inserting an NPA
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: rule out head and mid-face trauma, measure against the patient, use water-soluble lubricant, advance posteriorly rather than superiorly.
back.why_it_matters: The trauma contraindication and the direction of advance are what examiners watch for.

front.title: Suctioning
front.summary: In quiet, out sucking

back.body: Rigid tonsil tip for the mouth and thick material · Soft catheter for nose, stoma or through an adjunct · Measure corner of mouth to earlobe · Insert with suction OFF · Apply suction only while withdrawing · Max per pass: adult 15 s, child 10 s, infant 5 s · Reoxygenate between passes · Vomiting outranks everything else
back.why_it_matters: Suctioning on the way in is a critical fail, and bagging through vomit drives it into the lungs.

front.title: Suctioning the upper airway
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: eye protection, confirm suction at the tip, measure the depth, insert with suction off, suction only on withdrawal, keep the pass within 15 s adult / 10 s child / 5 s infant, reoxygenate between passes.
back.why_it_matters: Suctioning on the way in and running over the time limit are the two critical fails.

front.title: Suction limits
front.summary: How long, how deep, when the vacuum is on

back.body: Adult max 15 s per pass · Child max 10 s · Infant max 5 s · Depth: corner of the mouth to the earlobe · Suction applied on WITHDRAWAL only · Reoxygenate or ventilate between passes
back.why_it_matters: Running over the limit strips oxygen from a patient who had little to spare.

front.title: Choking: mild vs. severe
front.summary: The first decision is how bad it is

back.body: Forceful cough, air moving = MILD: encourage the cough, do not interfere · Cannot speak, cough or move air = SEVERE: act now · Over one year: abdominal thrusts · Under one year: cycles of 5 back slaps then 5 chest thrusts · Late pregnancy or too large to encircle: chest thrusts · Unresponsive: CPR, look before breaths, no blind sweeps
back.why_it_matters: Interrupting a working cough can turn a partial obstruction into a complete one.

front.title: Choking decision tree
front.summary: Air moving? Responsive? Under one?

back.body: Moving air and coughing forcefully → encourage the cough. Not moving air → responsive? If yes, under one year gets cycles of 5 back slaps then 5 chest thrusts, over one gets abdominal thrusts. If no, start CPR and check the mouth before each set of breaths.
back.why_it_matters: Three questions in order get you to the right action every time.

front.title: Abdominal thrusts, responsive adult
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: confirm the obstruction is severe, fist above the navel and below the xiphoid, inward and upward thrusts, switch to CPR the moment they go unresponsive.
back.why_it_matters: Landmark errors and continuing thrusts after the patient collapses are the two fails.

front.title: Oxygen cylinders at a glance
front.summary: Sizes, pressures, and the duration formula.

back.body: Full ~2,000 psi · Swap at 200 psi · D ~350 L (0.16) · E ~625 L (0.28) · M ~3,000 L (1.56) · Duration (min) = (psi − 200) × constant ÷ L/min
back.why_it_matters: The duration calculation and the 200 psi rule are guaranteed exam material and real-world safety.

front.title: Oxygen safety
front.summary: Oxygen is not flammable, but it makes everything else burn.

back.body: No oil, grease, or petroleum near fittings · Secure the cylinder · Away from heat and flame · Open the valve slowly, stand to the side · Check the hydrostatic test date
back.why_it_matters: A sheared valve turns a cylinder into a projectile; a greased fitting can ignite.

front.title: Nasal cannula vs. non-rebreather
front.summary: The two devices you will use on almost every call.

back.body: Cannula: 1 to 6 L/min · 24 to 44% · breathing well, mildly low sat · not for mouth breathers or distress. NRB: 10 to 15 L/min · up to ~90% · breathing adequately, needs high O2 · not for inadequate breathing (use BVM).
back.why_it_matters: Device selection is the single most-tested airway decision at the EMT level.

front.title: Nasal cannula
front.summary: Low-flow oxygen for the patient who is breathing well

back.body: Two prongs just inside the nostrils · 1 to 6 L/min · roughly 24 to 44% O2 · For adequate breathing with a mildly low sat · Above 6 L/min: switch device, don't raise flow · Useless for mouth breathers or a blocked nose
back.why_it_matters: The most common device you'll use, and the one most often used wrong by cranking the flow.

front.title: Applying a non-rebreather
front.summary: Six steps; four are critical.

back.body: 1. Confirm adequate breathing (critical) · 2. Set 10 to 15 L/min (critical) · 3. Fill the reservoir before applying (critical) · 4. Seal mask, tighten strap · 5. Bag must not collapse more than one-third; raise flow if it does (critical) · 6. Reassess SpO2 and work of breathing
back.why_it_matters: Skipping the reservoir fill or missing inadequate breathing are the two classic errors.

front.title: Non-rebreather mask
front.summary: High-concentration oxygen for the patient who is still breathing adequately

back.body: 10 to 15 L/min · Up to ~90% O2 · Fill the reservoir before applying · One-way valves keep exhaled air out · Bag must not collapse more than one-third · Inadequate breathing means BVM, not NRB
back.why_it_matters: The device-selection question between NRB and BVM is on every EMT exam.

front.title: Partial rebreather vs. Venturi
front.summary: Two masks you need to recognize but rarely use.

back.body: Partial rebreather: no one-way valve, some rebreathing, ~40 to 60%, 6 to 10 L/min, rare in EMS. Venturi: color-coded adapters, precise ~24 to 50%, flow printed on adapter, for controlled FiO2 (some COPD).
back.why_it_matters: The exam asks which device gives a precise concentration and what makes a partial rebreather different.

front.title: When the pulse ox lies
front.summary: Treat the patient, not the number.

back.body: Falsely high: carbon monoxide poisoning. Unreliable: poor perfusion, shock, cold, hypothermia, nail polish or artificial nails, bright light, motion. Normal SpO2 does not rule out inadequate ventilation.
back.why_it_matters: A 99% reading on a fire victim is a trap question and a real-world killer.

front.title: SpO2 ranges
front.summary: What normal looks like and where concern starts.

back.body: Normal: 95 to 100% · Concern in the acutely ill: below 94% · CO poisoning: reads falsely high, never trust
back.why_it_matters: The 94% line is where the oxygen decision starts.

front.title: Oxygen targets
front.summary: Oxygen is a drug. Dose it.

back.body: Most patients: titrate to 94 to 99% · CO2-retaining COPD: ~88 to 92% per protocol, never withhold in distress · High-flow without hesitation: hypoxia, shock, respiratory distress, inadequate breathing, CO poisoning
back.why_it_matters: Routine 15 L/min for everyone is gone; the exam tests whether you know why and who still gets it.

front.title: Oxygen is a drug
front.summary: Titrate it like one

back.body: Target 94 to 99% for most patients · Below target: give and adjust · In range and comfortable: no oxygen needed · Routine high-flow for non-hypoxic cardiac and stroke patients is no longer recommended · Hypoxia, shock, distress, inadequate breathing, CO: high-flow now
back.why_it_matters: Reflex 15 L/min for everyone is old practice, and the exam tests whether you know why.

front.title: Bag-valve-mask
front.summary: Breathing for a patient who cannot

back.body: Oxygen at high flow with the reservoir attached · Two rescuers preferred: one seals with both hands and lifts the jaw, one squeezes · Alone: C-grip, thumb and index on the mask, other fingers pulling the jaw UP into it · Squeeze to visible chest rise, then stop · A bad seal, not a weak squeeze, is the usual failure · The bag does not open an airway
back.why_it_matters: You are pulling the face into the mask, not pressing the mask onto the face.

front.title: BVM ventilation, apneic adult
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: open the airway first, insert an adjunct, confirm oxygen and reservoir, establish the seal, ventilate to chest rise only, reassess continuously.
back.why_it_matters: Sealing before opening the airway and over-squeezing are the two things that fail this station.

front.title: Ventilation rate
front.summary: Slower than your hands want

back.body: Adult with a pulse, not breathing: 1 breath every 5 to 6 seconds · Infant or child with a pulse: 1 every 2 to 3 seconds · Advanced airway during CPR: 1 every 6 seconds, compressions do not pause · Each breath over about 1 second, to chest rise · Too fast inflates the stomach AND reduces blood return to the heart · Count out loud
back.why_it_matters: Hyperventilation is an active harm, not just a wasted effort.

front.title: Ventilation rates
front.summary: The figures, and the ones deliberately left blank

back.body: See the numbers card: adult 1 breath every 5 to 6 seconds; infant or child 1 every 2 to 3 seconds; advanced airway during CPR 1 every 6 seconds with continuous compressions; each breath about 1 second to chest rise.
back.why_it_matters: The pediatric interval is roughly twice the adult rate, and using the adult one on a child is the classic error.

front.title: Is it working?
front.summary: Judge from the patient, not the bag

back.body: Adequate: visible chest rise and fall · appropriate rate · improving colour · settling heart rate. Inadequate: no chest rise · rate too slow or too fast · abdomen inflating · gurgling · audible leak. Reassess continuously — seals slip and heads move.
back.why_it_matters: The patient is the gauge. How the bag feels tells you nothing about what reached the lungs.

front.title: Gastric distention
front.summary: Air going down the wrong pipe

back.body: Caused by too much volume, too fast a rate, or an airway that is not fully open · Pushes on the diaphragm so ventilation gets harder · Big rise in regurgitation and aspiration risk · Fix with technique: slower, less volume, reposition · NEVER press on the abdomen · Cricoid pressure is no longer routinely recommended
back.why_it_matters: The instinct to squeeze harder is exactly backwards.

front.title: CPAP
front.summary: Support for a patient who is still breathing

back.body: Holds airways and alveoli open through the whole cycle · For an AWAKE patient breathing on their own, working hard, staying hypoxic · Classic: pulmonary edema, COPD exacerbation (per protocol) · Typical start 5 to 10 cm H2O, titrated per protocol · NOT in arrest, inadequate breathing, inability to protect the airway, vomiting, hypotension, suspected pneumothorax · Coach them or they will pull it off
back.why_it_matters: Every contraindication follows from one fact: CPAP supports breathing, it does not replace it.

front.title: CPAP vs. BVM
front.summary: Support versus replace

back.body: CPAP is for a patient who is breathing on their own and awake enough to cooperate; the BVM is for a patient who is not breathing adequately at all. Vomiting and hypotension rule out CPAP but not the bag.
back.why_it_matters: Choosing between them is really one question: is the patient still breathing adequately?

front.title: CPAP at a glance
front.summary: Pressure, patient, and the absolute no's

back.body: Typical start 5 to 10 cm H2O, titrated per protocol · Patient must be awake, cooperative, breathing on their own · NOT in arrest, inadequate breathing, unable to protect the airway, or vomiting · Also not in hypotension or suspected pneumothorax
back.why_it_matters: Every contraindication follows from one fact: CPAP supports breathing, it does not replace it.

front.title: Assisting ventilations
front.summary: Adding to their breaths, not replacing them

back.body: For breathing that is too slow, too shallow, or tiring out · Seal the mask, watch the chest, squeeze AS THEY BEGIN TO INHALE · Squeezing against their exhalation fights them and fills the stomach · Fast and shallow can move less air than slow and deep · When their effort fades, take over completely
back.why_it_matters: Timing matters more than force in this one.

front.title: Stoma ventilation
front.summary: The airway starts at the neck

back.body: Ventilate AT the stoma, not the face · A pediatric or infant mask often seals better on a neck · If air escapes from the mouth and nose, seal them and continue at the stoma · Stomas block with secretions — suction may be needed first · Head positioning does nothing here
back.why_it_matters: Everything you know about airways assumes the air goes in at the face. This patient is the exception.

front.title: Capnography
front.summary: Is air actually moving?

back.body: Measures CO2 in exhaled breath as a number and a waveform · Normal roughly 35 to 45 mmHg · A waveform proves ventilation is happening · Rising = ventilating too slowly · Falling = ventilating too fast · Sudden sustained rise in arrest suggests return of circulation · Capnography = ventilation; pulse oximetry = oxygenation
back.why_it_matters: Oximetry lags. Capnography does not — no air moving means no waveform, immediately.

front.title: Capnography numbers
front.summary: What the value is telling you

back.body: See the numbers card: normal 35 to 45 mmHg; rising means too slow; falling means too fast; a sudden sustained rise during CPR suggests return of circulation.
back.why_it_matters: In arrest, the number often moves before anyone can feel a pulse.

front.title: Asthma
front.summary: Trouble getting air OUT

back.body: Bronchospasm + swelling + mucus, all at once · Inhaling widens the airways, exhaling narrows them, so air gets trapped · Wheezing is mostly expiratory · A SILENT chest in a struggling patient is worse, not better · Judge severity by speech, accessory muscles, position, fatigue · Oxygen, calm, assist with their own inhaler per protocol
back.why_it_matters: The quiet chest is the finding that catches people out.

front.title: COPD
front.summary: Chronic, irreversible, usually from smoking

back.body: Emphysema: alveolar walls destroyed, lost surface area, lost recoil → pursed-lip breathing · Chronic bronchitis: inflamed airways, chronic mucus, productive cough · Most patients have both · Barrel chest, home oxygen, long smoking history · Assess against THEIR baseline, not a healthy one · Do NOT withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient
back.why_it_matters: The question is never whether they are short of breath — it is how today compares with their normal.

front.title: Emphysema vs. chronic bronchitis
front.summary: Two kinds of damage, usually together

back.body: Emphysema destroys the walls between air sacs and leaves the lung floppy, so exhaling becomes work. Chronic bronchitis inflames and clogs the airways with mucus, producing a long-standing wet cough. Smoking causes both, which is why most real patients are a mix.
back.why_it_matters: Knowing which is which explains why they breathe the way they do.

front.title: Pneumonia
front.summary: Infection in the lung tissue itself

back.body: Air sacs in one region fill with fluid and pus · Findings often LOCALISED — one area sounds different · Fever, chills, productive cough, pain worse on inspiration · Elderly may present only with confusion, weakness, falls, poor intake · EMT care: oxygen, position of comfort, transport
back.why_it_matters: An older patient who is suddenly 'not themselves' may have pneumonia and no fever at all.

front.title: Pulmonary edema
front.summary: A heart problem wearing a lung problem's clothes

back.body: Left heart fails → pressure backs up → fluid squeezed into the alveoli · Crackles, starting at the bases · Pink frothy sputum when severe · CANNOT lie flat — ask about pillows or sleeping in a chair · Look for JVD and swollen ankles · CPAP is the intervention, per protocol
back.why_it_matters: The pillow question is one of the most useful things you can ask.

front.title: Pulmonary edema at a glance
front.summary: The findings that make the picture

back.body: See the numbers card: crackles starting at the bases; pink frothy sputum when severe; cannot lie flat; JVD and pedal edema; CPAP per protocol.
back.why_it_matters: Five findings that together separate this from asthma and COPD.

front.title: Pulmonary embolism
front.summary: Air arrives; blood does not

back.body: A clot blocks an artery in the lung · That lung is ventilated but NOT perfused · SUDDEN onset, sharp pain worse on inspiration, fast heart rate · Lungs often sound completely CLEAR · Risk: recent surgery, immobility, long travel, leg clot, pregnancy, cancer · No EMT treatment: oxygen, position, go
back.why_it_matters: Clear lungs must not reassure you. The history is what saves the patient.

front.title: Spontaneous pneumothorax
front.summary: The lung peels off the wall

back.body: Air enters the space around the lung, the vacuum is lost, the lung collapses inward · Spontaneous = no trauma · Classically tall, thin, young, often a smoker · Sudden one-sided sharp pain and breathlessness · DECREASED breath sounds on one side · Watch for tension: worsening distress, falling BP, JVD, late tracheal deviation
back.why_it_matters: Listen at the same level on both sides — the asymmetry is the finding.

front.title: Hyperventilation syndrome
front.summary: The diagnosis you make last

back.body: Blowing off CO2 → tingling around the mouth and fingers, light-headedness, hand and foot spasm · A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION · Fast breathing is also PE, DKA, sepsis, poisoning, hypoxia · NO paper bag — it has killed hypoxic patients · Coach the rate down, oxygen if any doubt, transport
back.why_it_matters: Deciding 'just anxiety' at the front door is how a clot in the lung gets missed.

front.title: Epiglottitis and croup
front.summary: Two noisy children, one emergency

back.body: Croup: viral, builds over days, worse at night, BARKING cough, stridor, child still interactive · Epiglottitis: sudden high fever, DROOLING, muffled voice, sitting forward, will not lie down · NEVER inspect the throat or put anything in the mouth · Keep the child calm and with a parent — distress worsens obstruction · Oxygen however they tolerate it
back.why_it_matters: Calm is treatment here, not comfort.

front.title: Croup vs. epiglottitis
front.summary: Onset, cough, voice, drool

back.body: Croup builds over a day or two with a barking cough, hoarse voice, low fever and no drooling. Epiglottitis arrives in hours with a high fever, a muffled voice, drooling because swallowing hurts, and a child sitting bolt upright leaning forward. You never examine the throat of the second one.
back.why_it_matters: Four questions — how fast, what cough, what voice, are they drooling — separate them.

front.title: Respiratory infection precautions
front.summary: Do it the same way every time

back.body: Standard precautions on EVERY patient, before you know anything · Cough or fever: add eye protection and a mask · Mask the patient too where tolerated — source control beats provider protection · Pertussis: violent coughing fits, whoop in children · RSV: infant distress, little reserve · Influenza and COVID: mild to fatal · Report and document exposures
back.why_it_matters: By the time someone looks infectious you have already been breathing their air.

front.title: Assisting with an inhaler or nebulizer
front.summary: Their medication, your help

back.body: EMTs assist with the patient's OWN prescribed medication, per protocol · MDI: one measured puff, must be timed with a slow breath in · SPACER holds the puff so timing stops mattering — use for children and the very breathless · Nebulizer: mist over several minutes, nothing to coordinate · Six rights + check it is THIS patient's and in date · Reassess afterwards
back.why_it_matters: The hardest part of an inhaler is the timing, and the sickest patients are worst at it.

front.title: Assisting with a prescribed inhaler
front.summary: Critical steps and the common fails

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: protocol or medical direction, confirm it is this patient's prescription, check the expiry, run the six rights, reassess afterwards and document.
back.why_it_matters: Assisting with someone else's medication and not reassessing are the two fails.
